claims.text: The baseline alloy is equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered single-phase BCC solid solution.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has limited room-temperature compressive plastic strain.
The proposed intervention replaces approximately 20 at.% Mo with an equivalent amount of V while keeping Nb, Zr, Ti, and Hf constant.
The modified alloys will be arc melted and homogenized at 1200 °C for 1–2 hours under an inert atmosphere.
Replacing Mo with V decreases the electronegativity difference among the alloy constituents.
Decreasing electronegativity contrast favors retention of a single-phase solid solution.
The modified NbZrTiHfMo-V alloy will remain a disordered single-phase BCC solid solution without unwanted secondary phases.
Mo replacement by V slightly reduces lattice distortion.
Reduced electronegativity difference enhances dislocation mobility.
Enhanced dislocation mobility improves room-temperature plastic deformation.
Intrinsic solid-solution strengthening of the disordered BCC matrix will be maintained after Mo-to-V substitution.
The modified alloy will retain a compressive yield strength near 1719 MPa.
The modified alloy will exhibit approximately 20–30% greater room-temperature plastic strain than equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo.
The beneficial strength-plasticity effect exists only within a narrow substitution window.
Excessive Mo reduction or V substitution may destabilize the desired BCC phase.
Excessive Mo reduction or V substitution may reduce high-temperature performance.

contradictions.description: The change is called a partial Mo substitution, but equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo contains 20 at.% Mo, so reducing Mo by 20 atomic-percentage points and adding 20 at.% V would replace all Mo. If '20%' instead means 20% of the original Mo inventory, the modified composition would be different; the units are therefore internally inconsistent or ambiguous.
